notes:
Task and constraints: Return all distinct non-decreasing subsequences of nums with length at least two.
Idea: dfs(start) appends a copy of path once it has two values; it tries later indices only when the value is at least path[-1], using a local used set to skip duplicates at each depth.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking enumerates valid subsequences, and per-depth duplicate suppression prevents identical value sequences from being emitted through equal choices.
Invariant: path is non-decreasing, and it contains only elements chosen from indices earlier than the next search start.
Edge cases: An empty or singleton array yields []; [4,6,7,7] produces [4,7,7] only once; negative and repeated values work. path[:] is needed so later backtracking does not mutate saved answers.
Complexity: O(2^n) worst-case time and output space, since the number of subsequences can be exponential and each result is copied.
complexity_reason: The DFS explores include/skip choices across indices, and path plus recursion use at most O(n) depth while out stores every result.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return distinct non-decreasing subsequences of length two or more from nums.
Idea: dfs(start) copies path into out when its size reaches two, then uses a fresh HashSet at that recursion depth and adds only values at least the current tail.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking enumerates index-ordered sequences, while a per-depth set removes duplicate choices that would produce identical value prefixes.
Invariant: path remains non-decreasing, and each recursive call only chooses indices at or after start.
Edge cases: Empty or singleton arrays return an empty list; repeated 7 values are skipped at the same depth; the copy new ArrayList<>(path) preserves completed results. The set is recreated for each dfs call.
Complexity: O(2^n) worst-case time and output space because distinct subsequences can be exponential and each saved path is copied.
complexity_reason: Each recursive call scans a suffix of nums, and the path and call stack are at most n deep while out stores results.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count assignments of plus and minus signs that make the total equal target.
Idea: Compute total, reject impossible target ranges or odd total+target, then count subsets summing to goal=(total+target)//2 using descending one-dimensional dp updates.
Technique and why it applies: Transforming signed sums into subset sum allows a standard 0/1 count DP instead of enumerating every sign pattern.
Invariant: After processing a prefix of nums, dp[s] counts subsets of that prefix whose sum is s.
Edge cases: Target beyond total returns zero; an odd total+target returns zero; a zero-valued number doubles counts because it can be assigned either sign. Descending s prevents reusing a number within one iteration.
Complexity: O(n*goal) time and O(goal) space for n numbers and goal=(total+target)//2.
complexity_reason: For each number the code updates at most goal+1 DP entries in descending order, and dp has goal+1 counts.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count sign assignments on nums that sum to target.
Idea: Sum nums, reject an impossible target or odd total+target, set goal=(total+target)/2, then update dp[s] downward with dp[s-x].
Technique and why it applies: The sign-choice problem becomes a subset-count DP after algebraically separating positive and negative totals.
Invariant: After each processed number, dp[s] counts subsets of the processed prefix that total s.
Edge cases: An unreachable target returns zero; an odd total+target returns zero; zeros double dp counts because either sign yields the same sum. Java int totals and counts rely on the problem's constraints to avoid overflow.
Complexity: O(n*goal) time and O(goal) space for the one-dimensional dp array.
complexity_reason: The nested loops update up to goal+1 entries for every number, while dp stores goal+1 integer counts.

notes:
Task and constraints: For each nums1 value, return its next greater value to the right in nums2, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Scan nums2 left to right; while the stack top is smaller than x, pop it and record nxt[top]=x, then push x. Look up each nums1 value in nxt.
Technique and why it applies: A decreasing stack delays unresolved values until the first larger value appears, and a map answers the requested queries.
Invariant: When x is processed, every popped value receives its first greater value to the right; values left on the stack have not encountered one yet.
Edge cases: An empty nums1 returns []; a value with no greater successor maps to -1; a larger current value can resolve several stacked values. The usual problem guarantee that nums1 values occur in nums2 applies.
Complexity: O(n+m) expected time and O(n) space for nums2 length n and nums1 length m, since each stack value is pushed and popped once.
complexity_reason: The nums2 scan pushes and pops each value at most once, then the result comprehension performs one map lookup per nums1 entry.

notes:
Task and constraints: For each nums1 value, find its next greater element to the right in nums2, or -1.
Idea: Scan nums2, popping smaller values from st and storing their answer in next; then fill out by querying next for every nums1 value.
Technique and why it applies: The monotonic stack resolves values at the first larger element, while a hash map supports constant-expected-time query retrieval.
Invariant: When x is read, any value popped from st has x as its first greater value to the right.
Edge cases: Empty nums1 returns an empty int array; unresolved values use -1; one larger value may resolve several stack entries. ArrayDeque stores non-null integers, and nums1 values are assumed to appear in nums2.
Complexity: O(n+m) expected time and O(n) extra space for the stack, map, and output.
complexity_reason: Every nums2 value is pushed and popped at most once, and a second loop performs one map lookup per nums1 value.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return all matrix elements in diagonal zigzag order, alternating direction on each diagonal.
Idea: For each diagonal index d, compute its first valid row and column, collect values while moving down-left, reverse vals for even d, and append it to out.
Technique and why it applies: Diagonal grouping isolates cells with the same row-plus-column index, and alternating reversal creates the required zigzag.
Invariant: Each matrix cell belongs to exactly one diagonal, and out receives that diagonal's values in the direction determined by d parity.
Edge cases: An empty matrix or empty first row returns []; a one-cell matrix returns that cell; even and odd diagonals are reversed differently. The code assumes rows form a rectangular matrix.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space, with a temporary diagonal list holding at most min(m,n) values.
complexity_reason: The loops visit every matrix cell once across all diagonals, and vals temporarily stores one diagonal before it is appended.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return matrix entries in zigzag diagonal order.
Idea: For each d, collect the diagonal into v by moving down-left from its starting cell; reverse v for even d and copy values into out using p.
Technique and why it applies: Diagonal simulation groups cells by equal row-plus-column sum and reverses alternate groups to obtain zigzag order.
Invariant: p advances once for every matrix entry copied, so the output prefix contains exactly the diagonals already processed.
Edge cases: An empty matrix or zero-width first row returns an empty array; a single cell returns itself; even diagonals are reversed. The method assumes a rectangular matrix.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space, plus O(min(m,n)) temporary list space for one diagonal.
complexity_reason: Every cell is collected and copied once, and v holds at most one diagonal while out stores all m*n values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return words whose letters all belong to a single row of the American keyboard.
Idea: Build a row mapping from each lowercase letter to row index, then form the set of row ids for each word after lowercasing its characters; keep words with at most one id.
Technique and why it applies: A letter-to-row lookup converts the typing constraint into a set-cardinality check.
Invariant: For a word, ids contains exactly the keyboard rows used by its letters, so a size of one means the word is typeable on one row.
Edge cases: A one-letter word passes; 'Alaska' passes because its letters are in the home row; a word spanning two rows is excluded. Empty strings yield an empty id set and are accepted by this implementation.
Complexity: O(total characters) expected time and O(1) alphabet-map space beyond output, since each character gets one row lookup.
complexity_reason: The mapping is built for the fixed alphabet and every word character is lowercased and mapped once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return words typeable using letters from only one keyboard row.
Idea: Populate map for a-z from rows, then choose the first character's row and scan each word; add w only if all characters map to that row.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed row lookup turns the constraint into a linear membership test without checking all possible keyboard layouts.
Invariant: The boolean ok remains true only while every scanned character shares the initial character's row.
Edge cases: A single-letter word passes; a word with one letter from another row fails; empty strings would throw at charAt(0), so the implementation assumes nonempty words. Character indexing assumes English letters.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) extra map space apart from output, as the alphabet map has 26 entries.
complexity_reason: The code initializes a fixed 26-entry map and scans each word's characters until a mismatch or its end.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return all values occurring most often in a BST that may contain duplicates.
Idea: Inorder DFS visits values in sorted order, updates prev and count for each equal-value run, replaces out when count exceeds best, and appends ties.
Technique and why it applies: BST inorder traversal turns duplicate values into consecutive runs, allowing mode counts without a frequency map.
Invariant: count is the length of the current run of equal inorder values, and best is the largest run length encountered.
Edge cases: A null root returns []; one node is its own mode; repeated equal values increase count and can replace earlier modes. The code stores traversal state on self, so it resets fields at each call.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h+k) space for tree height h and k returned modes, with recursion stack and output storage.
complexity_reason: The inorder DFS visits each node once and maintains only run counters plus the mode list.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return every value with maximum frequency in a BST containing possible duplicates.
Idea: findMode resets prev, count, max, and modes, then dfs visits nodes inorder; equal values increment count, a new maximum clears modes, and ties append.
Technique and why it applies: Inorder traversal makes equal BST values adjacent, so a running count identifies the modes.
Invariant: count tracks the current repeated-value run, while max stores the longest run seen and modes stores values attaining it.
Edge cases: A null root produces an empty array; a single node is the only mode; a new larger run clears previous modes. Integer prev is nullable to distinguish the first visited node.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h+k) space for recursion height h and k modes, excluding constant state.
complexity_reason: Each tree node is visited once and added or compared using a constant number of counter and list operations.

notes:
Task and constraints: For every circular-array element, find the next greater value or -1 if no greater value exists.
Idea: Initialize ans to -1, scan indices from 0 to 2*n-1 using i%n, pop unresolved indices whose values are smaller, and push indices only during the first pass.
Technique and why it applies: A doubled traversal simulates wraparound, while a monotonic stack resolves each index at its first larger successor.
Invariant: Each index is pushed only in the first pass and removed when a strictly larger circular successor is found.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; a single element remains -1; equal values do not resolve each other because the comparison is strict. The second pass does not push duplicate indices.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space because the scan runs 2n steps and each index enters and leaves the stack at most once.
complexity_reason: The loop makes 2n iterations and each original index is pushed once and popped at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: For each value in a circular array, return the next strictly greater value or -1.
Idea: Initialize ans to -1 and scan twice using idx=i%n; pop indices from st when nums[idx] is larger, and push idx only during the first n iterations.
Technique and why it applies: Two-pass monotonic-stack traversal models the circular suffix without concatenating a second array.
Invariant: Every index is inserted into st once, and ans changes from -1 only when a strictly larger value is encountered later in circular order.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty array; equal values are not greater; a maximum with no larger successor stays -1. The loop avoids modulo by zero because it executes zero times for n=0.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for ans and st, since the scan has 2n iterations and each index is pushed/popped at most once.
complexity_reason: The scan runs twice over n positions, while each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a signed integer to its base-7 string representation.
Idea: Return '0' for zero; otherwise save the sign, take abs(num), repeatedly append num%7 and divide num by 7, then reverse the digits and prepend the sign.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated division extracts least-significant base-7 digits, which must be reversed to produce conventional notation.
Invariant: Each loop iteration removes the current least-significant base-7 digit by integer-dividing num by seven.
Edge cases: Zero returns '0'; -7 returns '-10'; positive numbers have no sign prefix. Python integers handle the magnitude of negative values without fixed-width overflow.
Complexity: O(log_7 |num|) time and O(log_7 |num|) space for the digit list and output.
complexity_reason: Each iteration appends one base-7 digit and divides the magnitude by seven until it reaches zero.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a signed int into its base-7 representation.
Idea: Handle zero directly; save whether num is negative, convert Math.abs((long)num) to a positive long, append remainders while dividing by seven, append '-' if needed, and reverse the builder.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated division generates digits from least to most significant, so reversing the builder restores standard order.
Invariant: At every loop iteration, x is the unconverted quotient and the builder contains the extracted low-order digits.
Edge cases: Zero returns '0'; -7 becomes '-10'; converting to long before Math.abs handles Integer.MIN_VALUE safely. The final reverse also moves a previously appended minus sign to the front.
Complexity: O(log_7 |num|) time and O(log_7 |num|) space for the StringBuilder and result.
complexity_reason: The while loop divides x by seven each iteration and stores one digit per iteration in StringBuilder.

notes:
Task and constraints: Assign medals to the top three scores and numeric ranks to all remaining athletes, preserving original input order in the result.
Idea: Sort original indices by score descending into order, allocate out, and assign a medal label or rank string at each athlete's original index.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting indices ranks athletes without rearranging the score list or losing the output's original positions.
Invariant: For every processed rank, out[order[rank]] stores that athlete's correct rank label.
Edge cases: One athlete receives Gold Medal; the second and third receive silver and bronze; lower scores get ranks starting at 4. Equal scores follow the sort's tie behavior, and the input score list is not mutated.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for sorted indices and output strings.
complexity_reason: Sorting n indices dominates, and the ranking loop writes one result per athlete.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return each athlete's medal or numeric rank in the original score-array order.
Idea: Create idx containing every original index, sort idx by descending score, then write medals or rank strings into out[idx[r]].
Technique and why it applies: Sorting indices lets the method rank scores while mapping each result back to its input position.
Invariant: At loop rank r, idx[r] identifies the athlete receiving rank r+1, and out is filled at that athlete's original index.
Edge cases: A one-element array receives Gold Medal; ranks after the first three are decimal strings; equal scores may be ordered according to object-sort stability. Integer.compare avoids subtraction overflow in the comparator.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the boxed index array and result array.
complexity_reason: The method sorts n indices and then assigns one label at each rank position.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return every subtree sum with the highest frequency in a binary tree.
Idea: DFS returns zero for null; otherwise compute node.val plus left and right sums, increment counts[total], and then collect sums whose counts equal the maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder traversal computes each subtree sum after its children, and a Counter tallies repeated totals.
Invariant: For each node, total equals the sum of that node and all descendants, and counts records how many nodes produce each total.
Edge cases: Null root returns []; a single node yields its value; equal subtree totals increase the same Counter entry. Python integers avoid sum overflow.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u+h) space for u distinct subtree sums and recursion height h.
complexity_reason: The DFS visits each node once and performs one Counter update per subtree, followed by scans over distinct sums.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return all subtree sums that occur most frequently.
Idea: Return an empty array for null root; otherwise initialize counts, compute each sum with sum(root), find the maximum frequency, and collect keys with that count.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder recursion obtains child sums before counting a parent sum, while a HashMap tracks frequencies.
Invariant: sum(n) returns the total value of n's entire subtree, and counts maps each computed total to its number of occurrences.
Edge cases: Null root returns an empty array; a leaf's subtree sum equals its value; duplicate sums share a map entry. Java int subtree sums can overflow if node values and tree size exceed problem bounds.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u+h) space for u distinct sums and recursion height h.
complexity_reason: The recursive sum method visits each node once, and two map scans find the maximum count and collect matching sums.
